title: Check if a string is a palindrome using streams.
shortTitle: Check if a string is a palindrome using streams
keyPoints: IntStream.range(0, n/2).allMatch(i -> s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(n-1-i)) checks a palindrome by comparing mirrored pairs
Only half the string is iterated because once the first half matches the second half, the whole string is confirmed
allMatch short-circuits on the first mismatch, returning false immediately
Normalize input by lowercasing and stripping non-letters for real-world palindrome checks

s1_definition.oneliner: IntStream.range(0, n/2).allMatch(i -> s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(n-1-i)) checks whether a string is a palindrome by comparing each character with its mirror.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Palindrome** is a string that reads the same forwards and backwards.
- **IntStream.range(0, n/2)** generates indices for the first half of the string.
- **allMatch** returns true only if every mirrored pair matches, and short-circuits on the first mismatch.
- **Normalization** means lowercasing and stripping non-letters before checking, so mixed-case input and punctuation do not cause false negatives.
- **No allocation** unlike the reverse-and-compare approach, which creates a new string.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya at the National Bank of India folds an account reference code in half and checks that the first character matches the last, the second matches the second-last, and so on. If every mirrored pair agrees, the code is a palindrome.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To test whether a string is a palindrome with streams, take the length n and iterate only the first half using IntStream.range(0, n/2). For each index i, compare the character at i with its mirror at n-1-i, and wrap the comparison in allMatch. The method returns true only if every mirrored pair matches, and it short-circuits on the first mismatch.

Iterating only half the string is correct because once the first half matches the mirrored second half, the entire string is confirmed. A single middle character in an odd-length string mirrors itself and needs no check. This is more efficient than reversing the entire string and comparing, because it allocates nothing and stops early.

In real-world use at the National Bank of India, Rajesh normalizes the input first by lowercasing and stripping non-letter characters before the index comparison, so that mixed-case codes and punctuation are judged on their letters alone. The half-range approach also handles edge cases naturally: empty and single-character strings come out as palindromes, which is the correct behavior.

Remember one sentence: IntStream.range(0, n/2) with allMatch compares mirrored character pairs, short-circuits on the first mismatch, and allocates nothing.
